clue.text: No decolletage for the girl athlete ?

definitions.text: No decolletage for the girl athlete ?

parts.words: No decolletage for the girl athlete
parts.note: a sweater with a high neck shows no cleavage, and the same two words name a sportswoman who clears the bar in a field event

explanation.walkthrough: 'Athlete' pulls toward sport alone; the clue also describes a polo-neck sweater, which hides any décolletage. HIGH JUMPER is both the garment and the competitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in the leaping event over a raised bar is named this, and a high-necked sweater is the same phrase.

clue.text: Prophet loses article in water-conduit

indicators.note: loses means the article is taken away from the prophet's name

parts.note: Hosea is a minor prophet of the Old Testament
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A biblical prophet drops an item into a water channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes the A off HOSEA.
explanation.definitionFit: A flexible pipe for carrying water is this.

clue.text: Like a night-light that's more than half full

definitions.text: Like a night-light that's more than half full

parts.words: Like a night-light that's more than half full
parts.note: the night-light is the moon, and more than half full is the phase between half and full

explanation.walkthrough: 'Night-light' suggests a bedside candle; it is the moon, between half and full.
explanation.definitionFit: The moon between half and full, with a bulging lit face, is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Potter's figure of Bentham wielding a rod?

parts.note: Jeremy Bentham was the philosopher who founded utilitarianism
an angler holding a fishing rod

explanation.surface: A philosopher is pictured fishing, as if in a children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Jeremy Fisher is the frog who goes fishing in Beatrix Potter's tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Jeremy Fisher is the angling frog in one of Beatrix Potter's children's books.

clue.text: Vehicle for boys only, we hear

definitions.text: Vehicle for boys only, we hear

parts.words: Vehicle for boys only, we hear
parts.note: a carriage for boys only would be a male cart, which is pronounced the same as a cart carrying post

explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' signals a sound-alike: MALE (for boys only) CART sounds like a cart for carrying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cart for carrying the post, or a light child's pushcart, is called this.

clue.text: They leave stage late, 'to ragged tune

parts.note: ex- means former, as late does in the late chairman

indicators.note: ragged suggests the word tune is torn about and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Performers walk off late to a scrappy melody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ragged' turns TUNE into EUNT. Exeunt is the Latin stage direction for several characters leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin stage direction means that the characters go off.

clue.text: Frankly royalist resistance units

definitions.meaning: On His Majesty's Service, the abbreviation stamped (franked) on official royal mail
the unit of electrical resistance, in the plural

explanation.definitionFit: Official mail is franked with the initials of On His Majesty's Service, and electrical resistance is measured in units named after Georg Ohm.

clue.text: Fish-for lady's circle

parts.note: her is the possessive for a lady
a ring is a circle

explanation.surface: A woman's circular piece of jewellery is sought.
explanation.definitionFit: A silvery shoaling sea fish of the North Atlantic is named this.

clue.text: Sewer has' the same trouble with compelling force

indicators.note: trouble means the letters of same are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: stress is pressure or force exerted on something

explanation.surface: A drain has the same problem with heavy pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain; it is one who sews. 'trouble' turns SAME into SEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who sews for a living is one who stitches clothes.

clue.text: Grave character of non-alcoholic aspects

parts.note: someone who has had no drink is sober
the sides of a question are its aspects

explanation.surface: A teetotaller is described as a serious-minded person.
explanation.definitionFit: A solemn, humourless person is called this, a serious type.

clue.text: 100 square metres — a measure of this

definitions.text: 100 square metres — a measure of this

parts.note: the are is the metric unit of land measure equal to a hundred square metres

explanation.surface: A metric unit is presented as a way of measuring surface extent.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the are is a unit used for measuring extent of surface, which is what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Units such as the are measure the extent of a surface, which is what this word names.

clue.text: Half the leaflet describes Norman arches

parts.note: semi- is the prefix meaning half
a circular is a printed leaflet sent round to many people

explanation.surface: Half of a pamphlet is devoted to Romanesque architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman (Romanesque) arches are round-headed, forming half a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman round-headed arches have the shape of half a circle.

clue.text: See, the morning earth!

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
a.m. is the abbreviation for the morning hours

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at the sight of the land at dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Rich soil made of clay, sand and humus is a kind of earth.

clue.text: Heap of eels that is taken, inside

indicators.note: the abbreviation is taken into the middle of the fish word, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: congers are large sea eels
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A pile of eels is described as having been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heap' is the definition, not part of the eel picture: congeries is a rare word for a jumbled collection.
explanation.definitionFit: This word means a disorderly collection or pile of things.

clue.text: Wastes make-up, going to dances where staff is exploited

indicators.note: make-up suggests the letters of wastes are put together in a new arrangement

parts.note: hops are informal dances

explanation.surface: Someone throws away cosmetics before going out dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make-up' looks like cosmetics; it is the anagram signal turning WASTES into SWEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Factories where workers labour long hours for low pay are places of exploitation.

clue.text: Congreve's lady is crazy for whist

indicators.note: crazy suggests the letters of the two card-game words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A character from a Restoration comedy is mad about a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Wishfort is the vain old widow in William Congreve's comedy The Way of the World (1700). 'crazy' rearranges FOR WHIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Wishfort is a character in Congreve's play The Way of the World.

clue.text: Down under the excavator

definitions.meaning: an Australian, from the old soldiers' nickname for Australians and New Zealanders
a machine or person that digs

explanation.definitionFit: Australians are nicknamed this, and a machine that digs is also called one.

clue.text: With federal government one's short of food.

definitions.meaning: under the Fed, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into UNDER FED: living under a federal government.
explanation.definitionFit: Being under a federal government reads as two words, and someone not given enough to eat is poorly nourished.

clue.text: Waylay a large number before the inn-sign

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
a bush hung outside was the old sign of a tavern, as in good wine needs no bush

explanation.surface: Someone is warned of a crowd waiting outside a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A bunch of ivy (a 'bush') once hung outside taverns to show wine was sold there.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait and attack someone by surprise is to ambush them.

clue.text: Sabre is: convertible into a club

indicators.note: convertible into says the letters of sabre is can be changed into another word

explanation.surface: A sword is claimed to be turned into a cudgel.
explanation.walkthrough: A brassie is an old name for the two-wood in golf, with a brass sole plate.
explanation.definitionFit: An old golf club, the number two wood, was called this.

clue.text: Take article and sell it back to WIndies

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: back tells us to read the letters of the two words sell it from right to left

explanation.surface: An instruction to buy something and resell it to the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SELL IT into TILLES. The printed clue says 'W Indies', the West Indies.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antilles are the island chain forming most of the West Indies in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Feminine form of Fidelio

parts.note: in Beethoven's opera the heroine disguises herself as a young man called Fidelio, so she is the woman behind that name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Feminine form' looks like a grammar question about the name; it is the heroine of Beethoven's Fidelio, whose overtures bear her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's heroine disguises herself as the youth Fidelio, so she is the woman behind that name.

clue.text: Learner and a high-class vehicle

parts.note: L is the learner-driver plate
taken as written
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A driving pupil gets a smart car.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's 'U and non-U' usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-wheeled carriage with a folding top is this horse-drawn vehicle.

clue.text: A deadlock on board, or the human factor in "Holy Deadlock "?

definitions.meaning: a chess position where the side to move cannot move legally, so the game is drawn
Holy Deadlock is A. P. Herbert's novel about a loveless marriage; a tired spouse

explanation.walkthrough: Holy Deadlock (1934) is A. P. Herbert's satire on English divorce law, about a couple stuck in a dead marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn chess position is called this, and a jaded husband or wife is a stale mate.

clue.text: Joyful cry of the blackbird

definitions.meaning: to exult or shout in triumph
a large black bird of the genus Corvus

explanation.definitionFit: A triumphant shout is this verb or noun, and the large black corvid bears the same name.

clue.text: Oddly enough. Eleanora, is '.employed

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed (scan confirms): 'Oddly enough Eleanora is employed (4)' for USED. 'employed' defines USED, but no parse of 'Oddly enough Eleanora is' gives USED: odd letters of the words do not give it and it is not hidden; the clue seems corrupt.

clue.text: Country house where hops take place

definitions.text: Country house where hops take place

parts.words: Country house where hops take place
parts.note: hops sounds like dances held at a country house, but the hops are the plants dried in a kiln building in Kent

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hops' suggests dances; it is the crop, dried in a kiln-house in the English countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiln building for drying the hop crop is called this.

clue.text: Eccentric society types?

parts.note: strange chaps, and also the members of a friendly society of that name

explanation.walkthrough: The Independent Order of Oddfellows is a British friendly (mutual-aid) society; its members are literally odd fellows.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a well-known British friendly society are called this, which also reads as strange chaps.

clue.text: Get rid of the outhouse

definitions.meaning: a small hut or storage building

explanation.definitionFit: To cast off something is this verb, and a garden hut is the noun.

clue.text: A northern port with a subterranean quarter

parts.note: S, south, is one of the four quarters of the compass
under the land, below ground

explanation.surface: A northern harbour town is said to have an underground district.
explanation.walkthrough: Sunderland is a port city in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunderland is a port city on the River Wear in north-east England.
